extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office examiners and patent practitioners (prosecutors/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and supporting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103, including how to identify motivation/suggestion to combine prior art, requirement for reasonable expectation of success, and how to treat claim limitations in obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art (must articulate)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on combining or modifying prior art, Office personnel must find (1) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (explicit or implicit) in the references themselves or in knowledge available to one of ordinary skill to modify/combine, (2) a reasonable expectation of success, and (3) whatever additional Graham factual findings are necessary to explain obviousness for the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate the three findings. Motivation can be explicit or implicit (e.g., market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings, known problems). If any of the findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used to support an obviousness conclusion. See cited case law (DyStar, KSR, Plantronics, Perfect Web).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine may be implicit and technology-independent
rubrics_metrics.description: A motivation to combine need not be express in the prior art; it may be implicit from background knowledge, the nature of the problem to be solved, or from general incentives (e.g., making a product stronger, cheaper, cleaner, faster, lighter, smaller, more durable, or more efficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether ordinary artisans would possess knowledge/skills to combine references. Improvements that enhance commercial opportunities or are commonsense may supply an implicit motivation. Provide a reasoned explanation even where common sense is invoked (see MPEP § 2143 and KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of desirable alternatives does not necessarily teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere disclosure of more than one alternative in the prior art does not constitute a teaching away from any of the alternatives unless the prior art criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prior art shows multiple alternatives, evaluate whether it actually discourages the claimed alternative. If the prior art as a whole suggests desirability of the claimed combination, that can provide motivation to combine even if it is not shown to be the preferred option. See In re Fulton and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where prior art teachings conflict, weigh the suggestive power of each reference
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more prior art references conflict, the examiner must weigh how strongly each reference suggests solutions to one of ordinary skill, considering the extent to which one reference accurately discredits another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the relative persuasiveness and comparability of the teachings (e.g., differences in experimental conditions may limit a reference's discouraging effect). Consider the degree to which one reference would deter an ordinary artisan from following another. See In re Young example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination/ modification alone is insufficient — predictability required
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that references can be combined or modified does not render the combination prima facie obvious unless the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a technique used in one device would predictably improve a similar device in the same way, § 103 may bar patentability. Conversely, unpredictability supports nonobviousness. Cite KSR and related authorities; provide reasoning tying predictability to the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions that claimed modifications were within ordinary skill require articulated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A bare statement that the claimed modification was within ordinary skill of the art is not sufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness; there must be articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conclusory rejections. Show objective reasons to combine teachings rather than asserting mere capabilities. Quote KSR: rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; rely on In re Kahn and related cases for required articulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification must not render the prior art unsatisfactory for its intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If modifying a prior art reference would render the prior art invention inoperable or unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, there is no suggestion or motivation to make that modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the modification would forego the benefits taught by the primary reference or make it inoperable. If so, that weighs against motivation to combine (see In re Gordon and related cases). However, simplicity of prior art alone rarely weighs against obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification must not change the principle of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the suggested modification or combination would change the basic principle under which the primary reference was designed to operate, the references do not render the claim prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the combination would require substantial reconstruction or redesign and a change in the underlying operating principle (see In re Ratti). If so, that argues against obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success is required for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is a reason to modify or combine the prior art to achieve the claimed invention, a claim may be rejected as prima facie obvious only if there also was a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable expectation does not require conclusive proof of efficacy; it requires at least some degree of predictability. Prior art that teaches enabling methods, or shows similar compounds/processes with predictable results, can support reasonable expectation. See In re Merck, Blanc, Acorda, Hoffmann-La Roche and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of unpredictability may support nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may present evidence showing there was no reasonable expectation of success; such evidence can support a conclusion of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider experimental or scale-up failures and relevant testimony demonstrating unpredictability in the art (see In re Rinehart, Amgen v. Chugai, In re O'Farrell). The burden is to show lack of reasonable expectation as of the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability assessed as of the time the invention was made (or effective filing date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an art is predictable or whether a proposed modification had a reasonable expectation of success is determined at the time the invention was made (or the effective filing date for FITF applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only knowledge and evidence available at the relevant time; later developments cannot be used to bolster an obviousness finding. See Ex parte Erlich and related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All words in a claim must be considered when judging patentability over the prior art; the subject matter of a properly construed claim is defined by its limiting terms under the broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider grammar and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill. When a claim requires selection from alternatives, the prior art teaches that element if any alternative is taught. If an independent claim is nonobvious, dependent claims are generally nonobvious unless dependency is improper. See In re Wilson, Gulack, Fresenius USA v. Baxter, and MPEP § 2111.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claim language that may raise limiting-effect questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claim language may raise questions as to its limiting effect (non-exhaustive): preambles; clauses like 'adapted to', 'adapted for', 'wherein', 'whereby'; contingent limitations; printed matter; functional language associated with a claim term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each such term in context to determine whether it is a true limitation. See cited MPEP subsections for guidance on interpreting these constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered and not ignored
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim is susceptible to interpretations, at least one of which renders it unpatentable, the examiner should reject for indefiniteness and also reject over the prior art under the interpretation that renders it applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base a prior art rejection on speculative claim meaning. Avoid piecemeal review by making both indefiniteness and prior art rejections when appropriate. Cite Ex parte Ionescu, In re Wilson, and In re Steele for limits on speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations unsupported by the original specification must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that do not find support in the original specification (new matter) still must be considered in the obviousness analysis and given weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore negative or other limitations simply because they lack specification support; consider their effect on obviousness (see Ex parte Grasselli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale supporting a §103 rejection may come from references, common knowledge, scientific principles, art-recognized equivalents, or legal precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale to modify or combine prior art may be explicitly or implicitly contained in the references, reasoned from general knowledge in the art, established scientific principles, art-recognized equivalents, or legal precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may invoke legal precedent and scientific reasoning when warranted, but must explain applicability to the facts. Avoid treating common rationales (e.g., automating a manual activity) as per se rules; tie the rationale to the case facts and provide a convincing line of reasoning (see In re Fine, In re Jones, In re Eli Lilly, In re Nilssen, Ex parte Clapp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of some advantage is the strongest rationale for combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: The most persuasive rationale for combining references is recognition that the combination would produce some advantage or expected beneficial result — e.g., making a product stronger, cheaper, cleaner, faster, lighter, smaller, more durable, or more efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An implicit motivation to combine exists when the combination yields a more desirable product/process even absent explicit suggestion. Explain why the combination would produce the stated advantage and how an ordinary artisan would perceive that benefit (see In re Sernaker, DyStar Textilfarben v. C.H. Patrick).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal precedent can support the rationale only if facts are sufficiently similar
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may rely on legal precedent to provide rationale supporting obviousness, but only if the facts of the precedent are sufficiently similar to the facts of the application under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply legal precedent consistently after considering all relevant facts. If applicant demonstrates criticality of a limitation, do not rely solely on a court's rationale that is factually dissimilar. Use In re Eli Lilly and other precedent as illustrations of appropriate reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale different from applicant's purpose is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason or motivation to modify a reference may differ from the inventor's stated purpose; it is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination for the identical advantage or result discovered by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ordinary artisan need not see the identical problem in the prior art to be motivated to apply its teachings. Consider broader problem contexts and permissible alternative rationales (see In re Kahn, Cross Med. Prods., In re Lintner, In re Dillon).
